title: Air-dry clay moon phase wall series
subtitle: Five slab discs tracing the lunar cycle, no kiln required
excerpt: Five circular discs arranged in a row mark the new moon, crescent, half, gibbous, and full moon phases. Each disc is slab-built in air-dry clay, with the lit surface area carved away to reveal the moon shape. No kiln is needed: the set dries at room temperature and hangs as a wall display.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles. Slab-building methods referenced from Encyclopedia Britannica 11th edition (1911) pottery entry. Lunar phase geometry derived from public domain astronomical diagrams.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat sheet of clay rolled to an even thickness, used as the building unit in slab construction
The drying stage where clay holds its shape but is still damp enough to carve and refine

content.text: Five circular
slab

discs, each 10 cm in diameter and 6 mm thick, map the lunar cycle from new moon to full and back. Each disc is a plain circle; the moon shape within it is formed by carving away the surrounding clay at the leather-hard stage, leaving the lit crescent or hemisphere standing proud on a darker painted ground. No kiln is needed: the full set of five dries at room temperature over two to three days and mounts on a wall with a small brass hook or hanging cord pressed in before drying.

materials.name: Clay slip (same clay body thinned with water)
PVA glue diluted 50/50 with water (for sealing)
Dark acrylic paint (for background ground coat)
Small brass picture-hanging hooks or twine (for hanging)

content.text: Preparation

Roll and cut all five discs in one session so they dry at the same rate and shrink to a matching size. Work on a canvas sheet or lightly dusted board to prevent sticking. Keep spare clay in a sealed bag throughout the session. Two 6 mm guide sticks laid either side of the clay help roll an even sheet.
Rolling and cutting the discs
Roll a portion of clay to 6 mm between two guide sticks. Aim for a slab large enough to cut at least two 10 cm discs from one sheet.

Cut a disc by placing a 10 cm circular template (a jar lid or a drawn card circle) on the slab and tracing around it with a fettling knife in one clean pass. Lift the disc onto a flat board dusted with flour or lined with paper to allow even drying.
Repeat for all five discs. Smooth any ragged edges with a damp pottery sponge immediately, before the clay stiffens.

Press a small loop of twine or a brass hook into the top back of each disc while the clay is still soft. The loop or hook should sit 1 cm below the top edge and be pressed in at least 8 mm deep so it holds once the clay is bone-dry.
Carving the moon phases
Wait until all five discs reach a firm
leather-hard
state before carving. At leather-hard the clay holds a clean cut edge without crumbling or smearing. Carving into softer clay tears the surface; carving into drier clay risks cracking the disc.
Disc 1, new moon: the disc stays fully flat. No carving needed. This disc represents the moon when no lit face is visible from Earth.

Disc 2, waxing crescent: draw a crescent shape on the disc face with a needle tool. The crescent occupies the right third of the disc. Carve away the remaining two-thirds to a depth of 2 mm using a fettling knife held at a shallow angle. The crescent area stays at the original 6 mm level.
Disc 3, first quarter: draw a vertical line down the centre of the disc. Carve away the left half to 2 mm depth. The right half stays raised.
Disc 4, waxing gibbous: draw a gibbous curve (the lit area covers roughly three-quarters of the disc). Carve the remaining quarter away to 2 mm. Smooth the carved area with a wooden rib.
Disc 5, full moon: no carving needed. The whole face is lit. This disc stays fully flat.
Smooth all carved edges with a barely damp sponge. Work in one direction only; scrubbing lifts the surface.
Drying

Leave all five discs on a flat surface to air-dry. Cover loosely with a cloth for the first 24 hours to slow the drying and reduce the risk of the edges curling upward. After 24 hours, remove the cloth. The discs are
bone-dry
when they feel pale, lightweight, and no longer cool to the touch. At this stage the clay is
greenware
: unfired but stable enough to paint and seal. Handle with care as bone-dry air-dry clay is fragile before sealing.
Finishing

Paint the carved background areas of the moon phase discs with dark acrylic paint, a deep navy, charcoal, or black, keeping the raised moon surface unpainted for contrast. Allow the paint to dry. Apply two coats of 50/50 PVA and water to all surfaces, front, back, and edges, allowing each coat to dry fully between applications. The PVA seal protects the surface and reduces dust absorption. The pale clay of the raised moon faces can be left natural or brushed with gold or pearl acrylic for a decorative finish.
Use and care

These discs are decorative indoor wall pieces. Air-dry clay is not waterproof: keep the set away from damp walls, windows that collect condensation, and direct water contact. Wipe the surface with a dry or barely damp cloth if dust accumulates. Do not hang in a bathroom or kitchen where steam is regular.
Variations
Make the set in three sizes: 8 cm, 10 cm, and 12 cm discs to create a graduated display. Arrange the five phases in a diagonal or cascading arrangement rather than a horizontal row.
Press star impressions into the carved background before it dries, using a needle tool or the tip of a pencil, to add a night-sky texture to the dark ground.
Use paper-clay air-dry clay instead for a stronger disc that is less likely to crack on the hanging hook. Paper clay also takes a sharper carved edge, giving the moon boundary a crisper line.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Disc edges curl upward during drying
items.cause: The disc is drying faster on the top surface than the bottom, pulling the edges up
items.fix: Cover the disc loosely with a cloth for the first 24 hours to slow drying. Flip the disc over after 12 hours so both faces dry at a similar rate

items.cause: Clay was still too soft when carving began, or too dry and brittle
items.fix: Wait until the clay is firm enough to hold a clean cut (leather-hard). Test on a scrap piece first: a clean line with no drag means the clay is ready

items.problem: Hanging hook pulls free before the clay is dry
items.cause: The hook was pressed in too shallowly, or the clay around it was too wet to grip
items.fix: Press a small coil of clay around the base of the hook and smooth it flat, adding more clay to hold the hook. Allow this repair to dry before handling

items.cause: The slab was too thick in the middle and too thin at the edges, creating uneven stress during drying
items.fix: Roll the slab between guide sticks next time to ensure even 6 mm thickness across the sheet. Repair hairline cracks in bone-dry clay with watered-down PVA pressed into the line

items.problem: Paint bleeds into the raised moon area
items.cause: The paint was too thinned or applied with too much pressure
items.fix: Use a fine-tipped brush for the boundary between the dark ground and the raised moon face. Apply one thin coat and allow it to set before adding a second
